findings.claim: “La Belle Dame Sans Merci” “begins and ends on the ‘cold hill side’ with ‘no birds sing’” (repeated in the L1 flashcard bank, the L1 four-mark scheme and the L7 model paragraph).
findings.truth: The bookend is “Alone and palely loitering … And no birds sing” (stanzas 1 and 12). “Cold hill side” appears only in stanzas 9 and 11, inside the dream.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg 23684, Keats's 1819 text: st.1 'Oh what can ail thee Knight at arms / Alone and palely loitering? / The sedge has withered from the Lake / And no birds sing.'; st.12 repeats it.

findings.claim: “Nettles” is “a single stanza of 16 lines in blank verse” (repeated in the L2 conclusion, two L2 mark schemes, the L6 form map, the L8 quotation bank and an L8 mark scheme). The glossary also defines blank verse as “unrhymed or loosely rhymed”.
findings.truth: “Nettles” rhymes ABAB CDCD EFEF GHGH in iambic pentameter, so it cannot be blank verse; blank verse is unrhymed by definition. The 16 lines form four hidden quatrains.
findings.evidence: LitCharts, 'Nettles' Form, Meter & Rhyme Scheme: 'a single stanza made up of 16 lines of iambic pentameter … rhyme scheme (ABAB CDCD EFEF GHGH)'. Poem Analysis agrees ('rhymes in an ABAB pattern … iambic pentameter').

findings.claim: “The final two lines — ‘My son would often feel sharp wounds again. / Soothing him into a survey of his injuries’”.
findings.truth: The last two lines are “Had called up tall recruits behind the shed: / My son would often feel sharp wounds again.” The second line quoted does not exist in the poem, and the order was reversed.
findings.evidence: LitCharts, 'Nettles' lines 14-16: 'But in two weeks the busy sun and rain / Had called up tall recruits behind the shed: / My son would often feel sharp wounds again.'

findings.claim: The nettles “regrown ‘tall as soldiers’” — a quotation used six more times across the unit (two L2 knowledge checks, an L2 flashcard, three mark schemes and the L8 memorisation bank).
findings.truth: “Tall as soldiers” is not in the poem. Scannell writes “tall recruits”; the other military words are “green spears”, “regiment of spite”, “fierce parade”, “funeral pyre”, “the fallen dead”.
findings.evidence: LitCharts full-text lines 14-16 and lines 9-12; Poem Analysis quotes the same wording.

findings.claim: “Nettles — Vernon Scannell (1962)”.
findings.truth: “Nettles” was published in 1980, in Scannell's New & Collected Poems 1950-1980.
findings.evidence: LitCharts, 'Nettles' Literary Context: 'English poet Vernon Scannell (1922-2007) published "Nettles" in his 1980 New & Collected Poems: 1950-1980.'

findings.claim: The child in “A Child to his Sick Grandfather” says “you shall have my chair” (also in the L2 four-mark scheme).
findings.truth: That line is not in the poem. The child's offers of comfort are “I'll lead you kindly by the hand”, “I'll with you bide” and “I'll sit and talk with you”.
findings.evidence: Poem Analysis full anthology text of 'A Child to his Sick Grandfather' (matches the Edexcel wording 'Your stocked legs begin to fail').

findings.claim: de Kok's repeated negatives are “would not show us” and “would not let us see” (also in an L2 knowledge check, an L2 flashcard and the L8 memorisation bank).
findings.truth: “Would not let us see” is not in the poem. The refrain is “My father would not show us how to die. / He hid, he hid away” and “My father could not show us how to die. / He turned, he turned away.”
findings.evidence: Revision World full text of 'My Father Would Not Show Us' (Edexcel Relationships notes), stanzas 5 and 7.

findings.claim: The lesson presents the poem as a father who hides “his emotional or physical vulnerability” and says de Kok describes “the father's body, his hands, his illness — that the children are not allowed to see or discuss”.
findings.truth: The poem is set at the father's coffin: the speaker looks at “My father's face / five days dead” and at the “unfrozen collar of his striped pyjamas”. The hiding is his dying (“would not show us how to die”), and “his hands” and the ban on discussion are invented.
findings.evidence: Revision World full text; the Rilke epigraph and the coffin stanzas open the poem.

findings.claim: Four-mark scheme quotes the child's “simple, monosyllabic vocabulary ('your head, it shakes so sore')”.
findings.truth: That line is not in the poem. The comparable line is “Your stocked legs begin to fail”.
findings.evidence: Poem Analysis full anthology text, lines 1-6.

findings.claim: “The four regular quatrains with an ABAB rhyme scheme” in “Neutral Tones” (repeated in an L3 mark scheme and implied by the L6 flashcard).
findings.truth: Every stanza rhymes ABBA (day/God/sod/gray; rove/ago/fro/love; thing/die/thereby/a-wing; deceives/me/tree/leaves) — an enclosed rhyme, which supports the 'trapped' reading better than ABAB.
findings.evidence: Hardy, Wessex Poems (1898) text via best-poems.net; all four stanzas checked line by line.

findings.claim: The fountain in “A Complaint” “never ceased to flow”.
findings.truth: Wordsworth writes “A Fountain at my fond Heart's door, / Whose only business was to flow; / And flow it did”. “Never ceased to flow” is not in the poem.
findings.evidence: Wikisource, Poems, in Two Volumes (1807), Vol. 2, 'A Complaint', stanza 1.

findings.claim: “One Flesh” opens “Lying apart now, each in a separate bed, / He with a survey, she with a book”.
findings.truth: Line 2 is “He with a book, keeping the light on late”; line 3 is “She like a girl dreaming of childhood”. There is no “survey” in the poem.
findings.evidence: Full text on internetpoem.com, best-poems.net and poetry.com, all identical.

findings.claim: Lucrezia de' Medici “died aged 17” (also on an L4 flashcard).
findings.truth: She was born on 7 June 1545 and died on 21 April 1561, aged 16.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'My Last Duchess': 'she died on 21 April 1561, at age 16'.

findings.claim: One practice question in every lesson is labelled “20 marks — Poetry Comparison” but sets a single-poem task and carries an 8-mark ladder (7-8 / 5-6 / 3-4 / 1-2). Eight questions in total: L1-L6 and L8 index 4, L7 index 3.
findings.truth: The board's anthology question is always a 20-mark comparison of two poems marked AO2 15 + AO3 5. These are house practice tasks worth 8 marks, so the label must say 8 marks and must not claim to be the board's comparison question.
findings.evidence: Spec, Component 2 Section B Part 1 and the comparison-marks table (AO2 15, AO3 5).

findings.claim: “The final one-word line — ‘Lethal’ (in some editions) or the knife image — ends the poem”.
findings.truth: “Lethal.” is a one-word line in the standard text of “Valentine”, not an edition variant, and it is not the last line: the poem ends “Its scent will cling to your fingers, / cling to your knife.”
findings.evidence: Standard text of Duffy, 'Valentine' (Mean Time, 1993); the closing stanza runs 'Take it. / Its platinum loops shrink to a wedding-ring, / if you like. / Lethal. / Its scent will cling to your fingers, / cling to your knife.'

findings.claim: Eddie Beddoes returned “with a bullet lodged near his spine”; the L4 flashcard glosses “foetus of metal” as “the bullet lodged near the soldier's spine”.
findings.truth: The poem places it elsewhere: “the foetus of metal beneath his chest / where the bullet had finally come to rest”. Published accounts of Beddoes say only that he was discharged with physical and psychological injuries from Bosnia.
findings.evidence: Armitage, 'The Manhunt', lines 15-16; PMT and St Bede's Edexcel notes on the poem's context.

findings.claim: The poet of “Love's Dog” is named “Jen Hatfield” throughout — 17 places across L5 (description, seven content blocks, conclusion, two practice questions, two knowledge checks, one flashcard), L6, L7 and L8.
findings.truth: The poet is Jen Hadfield. Note that the extracted text of specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md Appendix 3 also reads “Jen Hatfield”; that is a typo carried from the PDF. Every board-facing resource credits Hadfield.
findings.evidence: Save My Exams and Revision World Edexcel Relationships pages, and gcseenglishteacher.com's full text, all credit Jen Hadfield; Wikipedia and the Scottish Poetry Library confirm the spelling.

findings.claim: In “Love's Dog”, “Each stanza pairs something loved with something hated.”
findings.truth: Three of the eight couplets do not. “Its petting zoo / its zookeeper — you” is love/love, “its doubloons / its bird-bones” is love/love, and “burnt toast and bonemeal / bent cigarette” is loathe/hate. Two couplets also put the hate first.
findings.evidence: Full text of 'Love's Dog' at gcseenglishteacher.com (20 Feb 2017), all eight couplets.

findings.claim: “Hatfield (born 1978) is a Scottish poet”.
findings.truth: Jen Hadfield was born in 1978 to a Canadian mother and a British father and grew up in Cheshire, England; she has long been based in Shetland.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia and the Scottish Poetry Library biography pages.

findings.claim: Banned string: an AO code followed immediately by a full stop — “rich material for AO2.” in the L5 exam tip and “a point of comparison for AO2.” in an L6 collapsible.
findings.truth: The house validator rejects the pattern AO[1-4] followed by a full stop, so the whole unit fails validation until both are reworded.
findings.evidence: scripts/_validate_content_json.py BANNED_PATTERNS: re.compile(r"\bAO[1-4]\.[0-9]?").

findings.claim: “The sonnet … Two poems in the collection use it”, then lists “Sonnet 43” and “Neutral Tones” as “a modified sonnet-like structure”; the L6 flashcard gives that as the form of “Neutral Tones”.
findings.truth: Only “Sonnet 43” is a sonnet. “Neutral Tones” is four ABBA quatrains, 16 lines. Naming it as a sonnet form on a flashcard would cost AO2 credit.
findings.evidence: Hardy's text (see F10); spec Appendix 3 poem list.

findings.claim: Banned string: “Edexcel Component 2, Section B, Part 1 asks you to compare…” in the L7 opening paragraph, and “the Component 2 Section B Part 1 comparison” on the first L7 flashcard.
findings.truth: The validator rejects any “Component N” code, so the unit fails validation. The exam facts stated around it are correct (20 marks, AO2 15 + AO3 5, named poem printed, chosen poem from memory).
findings.evidence: scripts/_validate_content_json.py: re.compile(r"\bComponent\s+[0-9][a-z]?\b", re.IGNORECASE).

findings.claim: “Spend … 3-5 minutes checking for SPaG and missed AO3 opportunities.”
findings.truth: AO4 (spelling, punctuation and grammar) is assessed only on the first paper's post-1914 text question. This paper carries no SPaG marks, so time spent proofreading for them earns nothing.
findings.evidence: Spec assessment summaries: 'Marks will also be given for accurate use of spelling, punctuation and grammar' appears only under the first paper's Section B; the second paper lists AO1, AO2, AO3 only.

findings.claim: In the quotation bank, “‘Alone and palely loitering’ — devastation after love's loss (AO2: pathetic fallacy)”.
findings.truth: The phrase describes the knight, not the landscape, so it is not pathetic fallacy. The pathetic fallacy in the poem is “The sedge has withered from the lake, / And no birds sing.”
findings.evidence: Gutenberg 23684, Keats's text, stanza 1.

findings.claim: “Love's Dog” is said to be “built around a series of oxymorons”; the same label appears in the L5 key fact (with a dfn and glossary entry), a knowledge check, a flashcard, the conclusion and three mark schemes in L5 and L7.
findings.truth: The poem contains no oxymoron (two contradictory terms side by side). Its device is antithesis or paradox across paired lines. Two defensible options: (a) keep “oxymoron” as loose classroom shorthand, which several textbooks do; or (b) swap the term to “antithesis” or “paradox”, which needs the dfn, the glossary entry, one knowledge-check option, one flashcard and three mark schemes changed together. Recommendation: (b).
findings.evidence: Full text of 'Love's Dog' (gcseenglishteacher.com); each couplet sets one whole line against another rather than joining contradictory words.

findings.claim: Two mark schemes (L3 Q1, L7 Q1) offer “Hardy's … own unhappy marriage” as AO3 context for “Neutral Tones”.
findings.truth: Hardy wrote the poem in 1867 and married Emma Gifford in 1874, so the unhappy marriage came later. The poem was published in 1898, by which time the marriage was strained, so the link is arguable but a student who dates it to the marriage is wrong.
findings.evidence: Hardy, Wessex Poems (1898); the poem is dated 1867 in the collection.

findings.claim: “Love's Dog — Jen Hadfield (2012)”.
findings.truth: I could not confirm 2012. Hadfield's collections are Almanacs (2005), Nigh-No-Place (2008), Byssus (2014) and The Stone Age (2021); no source I reached dates the poem to 2012. Left unedited because I did not find the real date.
findings.evidence: Poem Analysis and Poetry Foundation biography pages list the collections but not this poem's first appearance.

findings.claim: A knowledge check asks students to complete “The named poem is _____ book (printed in the paper)” with “open”.
findings.truth: The whole paper is closed book; the named poem is simply reproduced on the question paper. The parenthesis makes the meaning clear, so I left it, but the word “open” sits awkwardly beside the correct closed-book rule taught elsewhere in the unit.
findings.evidence: Spec, second paper summary: 'Closed book (texts are not allowed in the examination).'

summary: Eight lessons checked against the spec and against the poems themselves. Twenty-eight findings: eleven fabricated or misquoted lines (Nettles, A Child to his Sick Grandfather, My Father Would Not Show Us, One Flesh, A Complaint), two wrong verse forms (Nettles is rhymed, not blank verse; Neutral Tones rhymes ABBA, not ABAB), the wrong poet name for Love's Dog (Hadfield, not Hatfield) in 17 places, two banned-string blockers that would fail house validation, and an 8-mark practice task mislabelled as the board's 20-mark comparison in every lesson. Every lesson carries at least one finding. The exam facts themselves are otherwise sound: 20 marks, AO2 15 + AO3 5, named poem printed, chosen poem from memory, closed book.
